highlights.title: Six green card holders in Texas charged in federal crackdown on illegal voting – US politics live
highlights.summary: Four illegal votes were apparently counted in error out of 11,388,670 votes placed in 2024 general election in Texas. Sign up for US Breaking News emails. Kash Patel, the FBI director, is now testifying before lawmakers on the Senate judiciary committee.
body: Earlier on Tuesday, Todd Blanche, the US attorney general, alerted reporters at the White House to stand by for what he called “a big development” in the federal crackdown on voting by non-citizens to be announced by Ryan Raybould, the US attorney for the Northern District of Texas.

When it came, however, Raybould’s announcement, that his office had charged six lawful permanent residents and one undocumented immigrant for voting in federal elections over the past eight years, hardly lived up to the billing.

While six of those charged cast ballots in the 2024 general election, the impact of their votes was almost immeasurably small, given that two of them cast provisional ballots that were not counted, and 11,388,670 other Texans voted in that election.
Donald Trump, whose false claim that voting by non-citizens is rampant inspired the investigation, won the state by a margin of 1,558,347 votes over his nearest rival, Kamala Harris.

highlights.title: We don’t need AI regulation — leave safety to us, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says
highlights.summary: AI isn't some new form of "alien mind," according to Jensen Huang. It's just hardware and software, so safety can be engineered by each AI product maker.
body: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang made his position on the dangers AI poses very clear while speaking at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference on Tuesday. To him, AI isn’t some new form of “alien mind,” as at least one OpenAI safety researcher has described it. It’s just hardware and software, he says, built by humans. That means, in his view, it can be controlled by humans and existing laws.

“Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one,” he said. “We’re developing software after all. We’re developing computing systems after all. It’s a complicated computing system, but it’s ultimately a computing system.”

Therefore, there’s no need for new laws or regulations to govern it, he argues. In fact, Huang sees little need for new laws at all. The free market, he argues, will be enough to pressure companies not to release unsafe products.

“If we’re not confident about the safety of the products, like all companies, like you and I, all the companies here, if you build a product or a service, and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability, or safety, then don’t release it. And so that’s a very obvious thing to do,” he said.

It's just hardware and software, so safety can be engineered by each AI product maker.

highlights.title: Brook, Buttler go berserk again as England thrash Sri Lanka in first T20
highlights.summary: ​​Harry Brook and Jos Buttler went berserk in a T20 at Southampton for the second time this summer as England smoked 254-4 against Sri Lanka during a 119-run win in the series opener - their first game since Kevin Pietersen's appointment as white-ball mentor.
body: White-ball captain Brook (114no off 49 balls) - who nailed six boundaries in one over - and predecessor in that role Buttler (80 off 44) plundered 128 from just 60 balls in partnership for England's second wicket once debutant Aneurin Donald (12 off 5) fell after slamming a six and a four amid a bright but fleeting cameo.

Brook and Buttler had combined for a riotous stand of 233 from 103 balls at the same venue in July as England romped to a total of 257-3 against India that secured a 4-0 series sweep, with Buttler tonking a century on that occasion and Brook an unbeaten 95.

highlights.title: As ‘American Idol’ Leaves Los Angeles for Atlanta, More Concerns Emerge About the State of Local Production
highlights.summary: Forget Hollywood. “American Idol” is heading to Georgia, dawg. In news that felt all too depressingly common in production-starved Los Angeles, word emerged Tuesday that “American Idol” — which has been broadcast live from Los Angeles since it originated in 2002 — would move production to Georgia.
body: The loss of more reality and game series production in California comes even as the state’s film and television tax credit program has expanded to include unscripted fare. But there’s a catch: Those competition shows must have a budget of more than $1 million per episode. That makes it difficult to qualify, even for major shows like “American Idol.”

The California incentives still don’t include docuseries, talk shows or game shows. States like New Jersey and Georgia, on the other hand, don’t limit their incentives. Georgia’s tax incentives require a total production spend of $500,000, making it more attractive for shows like “American Idol.”
“American Idol” was broadcast from Television City in the Fairfax district for most of its run; it later shifted to Red Studios Hollywood.
Deadline was first with the news about “American Idol’s” move to Georgia.

And while most of us know to cover the basics with smoke alarms, fire extinguishers and good locks, there are plenty of often-overlooked products that can leave you better prepared — from a fire blanket for quickly smothering a small fire to a leak sensor that alerts you when it detects water.
Below are 14 home safety and security upgrades worth considering once you’ve checked the basic boxes.

I’ve had a longtime fixation on fire safety dating back to childhood, thanks to a walkthrough house my hometown’s fire department set up to demonstrate common household fire hazards. highlights.title: AI ‘Actor’ Tilly Norwood Told Me That ‘All Lives Matter’
highlights.summary: The virtual character, which is promoting its upcoming movie Misaligned, tries to evade politics by repetitively commenting on the clothes you’re wearing.
body: For Hollywood stars, press junkets are an opportunity to promote new work while connecting with fans. They tell funny or embarrassing stories about one another, give us a glimpse into the film production process, and reveal mannerisms that make them more relatable.

So why would anyone want to talk to Tilly Norwood, an interactive, British-accented digital character and “actor” developed with generative artificial intelligence by Xicoia, an AI division of a studio called Particle 6 Group? It’s a fair enough question considering that it does not exist in our physical realm and will never appear in a movie that any halfway serious person would care about.

But Particle 6 recently claimed in an email that Norwood was “ready for absolutely anything!” What’s more, the company is allowing journalists access to the model without a handler to “keep the conversation on track.” So I decided to test whether Norwood could actually offer anything of substance.

highlights.title: ‘Love of Your Life’ Review: Margaret Qualley Goes on a Pretty but Surface-Level Healing Journey
highlights.summary: It would probably be glib to refer to “Love of Your Life” as “Grieve Pray Love.” Rachel Morrison’s film about COVID-era loss, recovery and renewal is serious in intent and earnest in execution, grounded by a performance of intelligence and emotional transparency by Margaret Qualley, and doesn’t…
body: Rachel Morrison's second film as director follows a young nurse, bereaved during the global pandemic, as she grieves, escapes and returns to herself.

None of this even remotely resembles real life, which makes Maya’s emotional recovery increasingly hard to map: We learn in passing that she’s somehow funding these extended, luxurious travels with a career segue into telehealth, and when her online therapist observes that “we’re really getting somewhere,” we just have to take her word for it. Cox’s script, meanwhile, trades increasingly in one-size-fits-all therapy speak, and despite Qualley’s natural sincerity as a performer, Maya seems steadily less specific a personality as the years pass.

Late in proceedings, “Love of Your Life” gets a welcome jolt of feeling and truth from a scene that reunites Maya with Ruth, beautifully played by Keener with all the shattered, visible exhaustion of a woman who hasn’t got to nurture her grief in the Algarve sun. As she unpacks her damage, frankly but no longer angrily, against the unphotogenic greige backdrop of her house’s timber siding, “Love of Your Life” finally reconnects with reality, and not a moment too soon.

highlights.title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
highlights.summary: Sam Altman and other tech CEOs say there are incentives to limit advancements in AI, as fears grow over the threats it poses to humanity.
body: OpenAI boss Sam Altman thinks people should have more faith in his company and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about all the risks.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

highlights.title: Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember isn't just a sequel - it's a culmination of everything Team Ninja has learned from Nioh, Ninja Gaiden, and Dead or Alive
highlights.summary: The original Wo Long is an overlooked gem. Fast-paced, brutal, and compelling, the game made a name for itself amongst hardcore action-RPG aficionados because of its key gimmick: that basically every single attack could be deflected.
body: And why is that? It's because of Ninja Gaiden. Wo Long 2: Wings of Ember was in development alongside Ninja Gaiden 4, and you can tell. There's a "three-dimensionality" in this title that was lacking in the first game. In Wo Long, I would jump into most encounters, mostly because the slightly dopey AI wouldn't see or hear me coming, and I could land a fatal strike. It was an instant win. In Wo Long 2, though, you need to use your aerial attacks; it's baked into the entire combat system.

Maybe Team Ninja has internalised the criticism of the first game a lot, because whilst you can still deflect most attacks, even trash enemies have special moves that need to be dodged or countered, not just deflected. As a result, you need to get pretty dexterous with your hands, hitting the right combination of shoulder buttons and face buttons in some kind of unholy medley of Guitar Hero and Simon Says in order to survive even the most bog-standard enemy. Hey, it keeps you concentrating. Predictably, then, the learning curve is much steeper than in either the first Wo Long or Nioh, but the payoff is also more sublime.

body: All of the remaining support acts on Ed Sheeran's US tour have quit, after the rapper Macklemore was dropped from the line-up for making pro-Palestinian remarks on stage.
Among them were Finneas, the brother of pop star Billie Eilish, who said in a statement: "Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed."
Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish band Lukas Graham also announced their departure. Irish folk band Beoga, who perform with Sheeran on stage every night, dropped out too.
The announcements came hours after Sheeran said he would not be drawn into a public debate over Gaza, and stressed he was not responsible for Macklemore being removed from the tour.

highlights.summary: National outcry against data center construction has spread to Philadelphia, where officials suggested possible construction in a neighborhood already impacted by a now-defunct oil refinery.
body: Across the country, Americans are debating how their lives might change if new AI data centers are built in their backyards. Data center companies and their customers are promising new jobs and economic growth, but that pitch hasn’t won over a majority of Americans who oppose data center construction in their area, often over environmental and energy concerns.
For activist Shawmar Pitts, these concerns aren’t theoretical. He knows better than anyone what it’s like to live in the shadow of American industrialization.

A lifelong resident of the Grays Ferry neighborhood in Southwest Philadelphia, Pitts grew up next to what was then the East Coast’s largest oil refinery, which shut down after an explosion in 2019. Though many of his friends and family suffered from chronic health conditions, he didn’t realize what might have caused these illnesses until he encountered the environmental justice group Philly Thrive, which was tabling in his neighborhood in 2018 about a proposed oil refinery expansion.
points: National outcry against data center construction has spread to Philadelphia, where officials suggested possible construction in a neighborhood already impacted by a now-defunct oil refinery.

highlights.title: 'This Is a Place You Come to Work Hard' — Wardogs CEO Justifies Crunch as a Balancing Act
highlights.summary: Joe Brammer, the CEO of Wardogs developer Bulkhead, has stated that the studio avoids hiring people who aren't willing to crunch. In an interview with The Game Business, Brammer was asked about the studio's approach to crunch. He noted that he values balance, but not in the way people may think.
body: "For the last three months, Wardogs has been a lot more important than a lot of their family lives," said Brammer. "It has been, because that's what pays the money for them. But now Bulkhead has to acknowledge that it needs to go the other way. For example, everyone is pushing us to get console out earlier.

"We've just said, 'No, you don't understand, that's not how it's going to work. We can't push them more. We're not doing that. It's going to release in 2028 when we say it's going to release.' So, for me it's about balance and helping people and making sure they have a company where they can say, 'I'm tapping out,' and not feel like they're going to get fired for tapping out."

Brammer went on to note that it has become harder to crunch due to the team getting older and trying to start families. He stated that they initially offered 10-week paternity leave, but eventually had to ditch it because the employees' partners were struggling to handle them going back to work. Instead, Bulkhead now offers 2-weeks of paternity leave and gives half-days to employees as a way of making the transition easier for the families.

body: Sandra is in rehearsals for her Broadway return in Brecht’s Mother Courage — and therein lies the first clue to her festering secret — but the seasoned pro is having uncharacteristic trouble remembering her lines and motivation. Nonetheless, she sends out formal invitations to her estranged family to attend the play’s opening.

Her jittery sister April ( Naomi Watts ) bristles at being “summoned” to a reunion after three decades of silence. But she can’t get there fast enough, concerned that her rudderless son Theo ( Toby Wallace ), who’s living in New York, should be kept away from his self-absorbed aunt. Before April can run interference, Theo drops a bombshell by revealing that he has already connected with the black-sheep diva. The scowling posters of Aunt Sandra all over town suggest that encounter was all but preordained.

April and Sandra’s tart-tongued, boozing mother Diane ( Dianne Wiest, in brilliant form) takes a hard pass on the trip from their distant hometown, where she owns a shabby hair salon. But once April starts reporting back, the blowzy old woman — still pissed about Sandra sleeping with April’s boyfriend when she was 15 — hops on a plane.

highlights.title: How Mariska Hargitay Pulled Off Her Fashion-Filled 2026 Emmys Hosting Gig
highlights.summary: “Let’s be honest, it’s a little terrifying,” says Harigtay of hosting. “But I’m in a season of my life where I’ve been presented with opportunities that terrified me a bit, so I thought, why not!”
body: Given the fact that Mariska Hargitay has been steering Law & Order: SVU for 27 years (!!) now, it’s safe to say she was the perfect choice to host the 2026 Emmys last night. She is, after all, a TV legend.

There was even more to celebrate: Hargitay was also the first woman to host the Emmys in 15 years. “When I first heard that, I was genuinely surprised,” Hargitay tells Vogue post-event. “Of course I understand the significance of it, and I’m incredibly proud to be that woman. But I also hope the next woman doesn’t have to wait another 15 years. There are so many brilliant, funny, fearless women who could stand on that stage.”

Her opening monologue certainly did not disappoint. “NBC is celebrating its 100th year, and I’ve been on Law & Order for all of them,” was one of many zingers. There were skits with Taylor Swift, and even a musical number with Andrew Rannells. “I love television,” Hargitay says. “I’ve spent so much of my life making it, and I very much understand how many people it takes to tell these stories and make them matter. So the idea of getting to stand in that room, and celebrate this community, felt incredibly special.”

highlights.summary: Poll data released Tuesday by the New York Times and Siena University confirms what we've already been seeing, and what politicians are responding to - AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular.
body: 61 percent of likely voters said they oppose the construction of AI data centers, but neither major party has much of an edge.

56 percent of voters surveyed who said they were opposed to data centers said they supported limits, while 38 percent instead preferred a total ban. The list of reasons for opposition is also revealing, with the environment/water usage most common at 32 percent, impact on local communities at 21 percent, general distrust or dislike of AI at 18 percent, followed by regulation concerns and the economy at 10 and 9 percent.
An NBC News poll in March showed AI polling lower than ICE, and a Gallup poll in May revealed seven in ten Americans opposed local construction of AI data centers.

highlights.title: Marvel's Wolverine Offers Up a Canonical Explanation for Why Logan's Costume Regenerates
highlights.summary: Marvel's Wolverine explains why Logan's clothes can heal, just like his body. Near the beginning of Marvel's Wolverine, Logan is gifted a proper superhero suit from Walter Langkowski. It's Wolverine's signature suit from the comics, cowl and all.
body: However, this isn't just any ordinary nano-tech: it's Phalanx. In Marvel lore, Phalanx are a cybernetic species that go up against the X-Men and other heroes. They use their techno-organic lifeforms to infect other species and create a hivemind. Whether this has any larger implications remains to be seen, but it's likely more of a fun way to explain things to fans using established material from the Marvel universe. In the MCU, nano-tech is extremely popular and is used prominently by Iron Man, Spider-Man, Black Panther, and the entire Avengers team in Endgame. It's nifty, though some feel like the films have begun to over-rely on it for suits.

In X-Men Origins: Wolverine, a game that Insomniac's new title takes a lot of inspiration from, Logan's wounds would also heal when out of combat. This sometimes meant that his clothes would re-generate too, but there wasn't really an in-universe reason for this, though no one seemed to care back then.

highlights.summary: “The Julia Set” has emerged as one of the biggest surprises of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival. In her feature debut, writer-director Niki Byrne crafted a perfect showcase for the talents of “One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti.
body: Niki Byrne: Everything I’ve done makes sense in reverse. I came back to California from Europe in 2018 and started working in L.A. I was writing quite a bit at that point, and I knew I wanted to write and direct. I took Martin Scorsese’s master class, where he said that if you’re going to be a director of any quality, you must take acting classes. So, I did and found it super valuable. I’ve worked in almost every department on a film set and found acting incredibly difficult.

NB: When acting is done poorly, it’s the easiest job on set. When it’s done well, it’s by far the hardest. I wrote this movie during [COVID] lockdown and came out with this sort of weird confessional script and linked arms with [my producers], and we went on the hunt for our Julia. Then this one walked into a coffee shop in Koreatown.

Chase Infiniti: Three years ago. I was a month into shooting “Presumed Innocent.” And you did “One Battle After Another” between then and now, crazy. One of the things that struck me about this performance is how restrained your character is – even in the face of serious abuse and mistreatment from people and systems.

highlights.title: The Roman telescope has enough gas for 22 years, double NASA's expectations
highlights.summary: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is gliding toward its distant observation post on a pinpoint trajectory so precise that engineers estimate the spacecraft's fuel load will last twice as long as their initial expectations, the space agency confirmed Monday.
body: The $4.3 billion observatory’s designers originally planned to load enough propellant into Roman’s four fuel tanks for a minimum lifetime of five years, plus a potential five-year mission extension. That was a conservative estimate. NASA officials knew an on-target launch and perfect execution of the observatory’s first post-launch course correction maneuver would leave Roman with a hearty fuel reserve.

“As a result of exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team, brilliant execution by the operations team, and a precise launch from SpaceX, Roman has fuel for at least 22 years of potential science operations,” Jamie Dunn, center director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, said in a press release.
The James Webb Space Telescope received a similar lifetime boost after a picture-perfect launch on a European Ariane 5 rocket in 2021.

highlights.title: With ‘Book of Hours,’ Ellen O’Connell Whittet Finds a New Path to Justice
highlights.summary: Ellen O’Connell Whittet speaks to Vogue about how her Catholic upbringing informed her experiences with pregnancy; fictionalizing her own story; and finding new paths to justice outside of the law.
body: At the beginning of the pandemic, author Ellen O’Connell Whittet was preparing to publish her first book and give birth to her first child. By the time her memoir, What You Become in Flight, hit shelves that April, Whittet had told her entire life story—including her challenges with an eating disorder and a ballet career cut short—with no idea what lay ahead.

When Whittet experienced an act of obstetric violence during her already arduous labor, she knew that she would one day write about it. But, she realized, the story would perhaps be better told in a work of fiction. The result is Book of Hours, out today from Dzanc Books, in which Whittet weaves together the violence that she experiences at the hands of her doctor with her protagonist’s visions of canonized saints.
“I am very clearly not the person that I’m writing about,” she says. “But [that] I could give the experience to somebody that feels like justice.”
Vogue: When did you know that you were going to write about your birth experience? When did you feel ready to write about it?
